title: Can these bones live? (Ezekiel 37:1–14)
hookLine: the valley of dry bones, read on the Shabbat of Passover
last: FLESH IS MORE VULNERABLE THAN STONE.

cards: The hand of the Lord takes hold of Ezekiel and sets him down in the middle of a valley, and the valley is full of bones.
He's led around them, round about, the text says, and he sees there are very many, and they are very dry. Not a fresh battlefield: bones bleached and scattered, long past anyone's grief.
And then comes the question, put to the prophet as he stands there: "Son of man, can these bones live?"

teach.b: Ezekiel's answer is short and honest: "O Lord GOD, thou knowest." Not yes, not no. He hands the question back.
Then he's told to speak to the bones: "O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD."

teach.h: BONE TO ITS BONE, BUT NO BREATH.
teach.b: As he speaks, there is a noise, a shaking, and the bones come together, bone to its bone. Sinews come, then flesh, then skin covers them. And the text stops on a chilling detail: there was no breath in them.
So he's told to speak a second time, to the wind, the breath. The chapter keeps returning to one Hebrew word, ruach, and the King James renders it breath, wind and spirit.

teach.h: COME FROM THE FOUR WINDS, O BREATH.
teach.b: Come from the four winds, O breath. The breath comes into them, and they live, and stand up on their feet, a great army. Then the chapter says what the vision means.

teach.h: OUR HOPE IS LOST, AND THE ANSWER.
teach.b: These bones are the whole house of Israel, saying: "Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost." And the answer: I will open your graves, and bring you into the land of Israel, and put my spirit in you, and you shall live.
Some readers hear in it the return of an exiled people to their land. Others hear a promise of the resurrection of the dead, a belief Jewish prayer holds.

The rabbis of the Talmud even argued about whether it really happened or was a parable. And Jews read this chapter in synagogue on the Shabbat that falls during Passover, the festival of a people brought out alive.

how: Jews read Ezekiel 37:1–14 as the prophetic reading on the Shabbat during Passover, and Jewish prayer speaks of God who gives life to the dead.

o: the bones of the dead, waiting in the grave
a valley where an old battle was fought
breath, wind and spirit, all in one word

games.q: can these bones live — tap the pairs.
p: what the house of Israel says

s: the bones live as soon as they come together

the chapter explains its own vision

games.q: you're Ezekiel, standing in a valley of dry bones. you're asked: can these bones live? what do you say?
games.why: he hands the question back. then he is told to speak to the bones, and later to the breath, and they live.

practice: Sit still first, like the bones before the breath came, and let four breaths arrive on their own: ruach, the word the chapter keeps using.
Then bring to mind one thing you've written off, a skill your hands used to know, a song you stopped singing, and ask honestly: can this live?
You don't have to answer; you can say what Ezekiel said, thou knowest, and if you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Ruach. Hebrew for breath, wind, spirit: the question put to Ezekiel in a valley of dry bones, before it comes into them and they stand. Today's word.
